name: David E. Scull
bio: David E. Scull was a Quaker printer of Annandale, Virginia, who refused to answer 31 questions put to him by the Virginia Legislative Committee on Law Reform and Racial Activities — a 'massive resistance' body — about his ties to the NAACP, B'nai B'rith, the ACLU and his contributions to school-integration suits. Found guilty of contempt and sentenced to 10 days in jail and a $50 fine, he appealed to the Supreme Court in the landmark Scull v. Virginia.
charges: Contempt of a Virginia legislative committee — refusing to answer 31 questions
convicted: Found guilty of contempt; appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court
sentence: 10 days in jail and a $50 fine

name: Mathilda Carman
bio: Mathilda Carman was a New York City Department of Welfare case worker convicted of perjury in November 1957 for denying Communist affiliations before Mayor Wagner's Investigation Commission. Detectives had forced their way into her home to arrest her; sentenced to 60 days, she fought the New York Security Risk Law on appeal before the Appellate Division.
charges: Perjury under the New York Security Risk Law — denying Communist affiliations in a loyalty probe

name: Maurice McCrackin
bio: The Rev. Maurice McCrackin was a Cincinnati minister who for ten years refused to pay federal income taxes because he would not 'buy guns or bombs.' In 1958 federal agents carried him bodily before a commissioner; indicted in November, he was jailed for an indefinite contempt term, went on a hunger strike, and on Dec. 12 was convicted of refusing an IRS summons and sentenced to six months and a $250 fine.
charges: Refusing an IRS summons; contempt of court (war-tax resistance)

name: Emmett Calvin Brown
bio: Emmett Calvin Brown was convicted of contempt for declining to answer the questions of the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission. He was one of the appellants in the case that reached the U.S. Supreme Court as Raley v. Ohio, which turned on the commission's failure to honor the witnesses' invocation of their rights.
charges: Contempt — refusing to answer the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission
sentence: Convicted of contempt; case taken to the Supreme Court (Raley v. Ohio)

name: Thomas Raley
bio: Thomas Raley refused to answer questions before the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission and was convicted of contempt. His appeal, joined with those of his co-defendants, became the landmark Raley v. Ohio (1959), in which the Supreme Court overturned the convictions because the commission had misled the witnesses about their right to remain silent.
charges: Contempt — refusing to answer the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission
sentence: Convicted of contempt; lead appellant in Raley v. Ohio

name: Joseph Stern
bio: Joseph Stern was convicted of contempt for declining to answer the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission, one of the co-appellants with Thomas Raley and Emmett Calvin Brown whose cases the Supreme Court reversed in Raley v. Ohio.
charges: Contempt — refusing to answer the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission
sentence: Convicted of contempt; co-appellant in Raley v. Ohio

name: Norton Anthony Russell
bio: Norton Anthony Russell was an engineer of Yellow Springs, Ohio, and one of eight people whose contempt-of-Congress convictions — for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee — were on appeal before the U.S. Court of Appeals in 1958, in the wave of cases that followed the Supreme Court's Watkins decision.
charges: Contempt of Congress — refusing to answer HUAC
sentence: Convicted of contempt of Congress; appealing

name: Bernhard Deutch
bio: Bernhard Deutch, a former University of Pennsylvania student, was one of eight people whose contempt-of-Congress convictions for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee were pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals in 1958, alongside those of Arthur Miller, John T. Gojack and others.
charges: Contempt of Congress — refusing to answer HUAC
sentence: Convicted of contempt of Congress; appealing
